Chapter 7: Encouraging Social Connection and Cooperation
When you think about yoga, you might picture a quiet, solo practice. But for young kids, yoga can actually be a wonderful way to connect with others—to build social skills, and to feel like they truly belong.
Doing yoga together—whether it’s with a friend, in a small group, or as a family—creates all sorts of opportunities for cooperation, empathy, and shared joy.
The real magic of social connection in yoga is pretty simple: it’s about moving and breathing together. Kids learn to notice each other, take turns, and support one another—sometimes without even realizing it.
So, what does that actually look like?
Sometimes, it’s partner poses—maybe balancing together, holding hands, or mirroring each other’s movements. Other times, it’s about group games: forming shapes as a team, passing a soft ball while breathing, or creating a “yoga train” that winds across the room. And don’t forget about those special shared rituals—like starting and ending each session with a group breath, a song, or just a gentle touch.
These playful activities give kids a chance to practice important social skills in a really low-pressure way. Partner poses, for example, need both communication and trust. Group games encourage everyone to listen, cooperate, and celebrate each other. And when adults join in and model kindness and respect, they can gently guide kids to notice how their actions affect others.
Yoga is also a beautiful way for kids to celebrate what makes them unique. Every child’s body moves a little differently, and there’s really no one “right” way to participate. By honoring each person’s unique abilities and choices, yoga helps create a culture of inclusion and acceptance.
If you want to nurture social connection through yoga, here are a few ideas you might try:
First, encourage teamwork. Maybe work together to create a group pose or come up with a new sequence.
Next, practice a little gratitude. Try sharing something you appreciate about a partner, or about the group as a whole.
And finally, take a moment to reflect on feelings. After a session, ask, “How did it feel to move together?” You might be surprised at what comes up.
These shared experiences help build trust and friendship, making every child feel seen and valued in the group. And that, at the end of the day, is one of the greatest gifts yoga can offer.
